evening.title: Autonomous Cessna Caravan Air Ambulance To Be Tested By U.S. Military
evening.text:
U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) is set to demonstrate a potential autonomous casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) capability in Morocco. The test will involve a Cessna Model 208B Grand Caravan with an artificial intelligence (AI) driven ‘copilot’ from Merlin Labs.

The ability to send out pilot-optional or even entirely uncrewed aircraft to rescue injured personnel could be extremely valuable for supporting U.S. operations in Africa. American forces on that continent are routinely deployed in remote areas where immediate access to medical care can be very limited. Autonomous CASEVAC capabilities could also be very relevant in other locales, like the Pacific, where future operations could be widely spread out across constellations of small islands.

Merlin Labs announced the planned capability demonstration today, which is being conducted under the initial phase of AFRICOM’s Autonomous Casualty Evacuation (CASEVAC) Industry Technology Challenge. The test is currently scheduled for some time in “early U.S. government fiscal year 2027.” That fiscal cycle began on October 1.

“The demonstration will encompass the full mission, from initial tasking and flight planning continuing through autonomous departure and enroute flight to an austere casualty collection site,” according to Merlin’s release. “Following simulated patient loading, the aircraft will conduct its return mission, autonomously completing the flight and landing back at the designated location.”

AFRICOM has awarded Merlin a very small $500,000 contract to support this demonstration. The company has already received millions of dollars in funding from the U.S. military for separate autonomy projects. This includes the development of autonomous capabilities for C-130-type aircraft for U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM) and similar efforts in support of the U.S. Air Force’s KC-135 tanker fleet. Just yesterday, Merlin announced a new deal with SOCOM, valued at $8.9 million, for continued C-130 autonomy work.

Merlin has said previously that its flagship autonomy package, called Merlin Pilot, has flown on at least four different types of aircraft already. Merlin Pilot is designed to be scalable in form and function, and can be configured to enable pilot-optional flight capability. The system can also increase safety margins during crewed flight operations by reducing task burdens (and resulting fatigue) for the humans onboard and helping alert them to potential technical faults.

“Merlin’s demonstration [for AFRICOM] is planned to show how Merlin Pilot can bring onboard autonomy to aircraft supporting CASEVAC missions, managing flight planning, navigation, contingency response and mission completion without relying on a remote ground station or flight crew,” the release adds. “The system is designed to plan the optimal route from an operator’s tasking, replan dynamically around hazards, communicate with air traffic control using natural language processing, and continue safely along its authorized plan if a communications link is lost.”

The Grand Caravan’s “large cargo door and flat-floor cabin will allow ground level litter loading without rotor wash, winching or special equipment, and its cabin will be configured with an air ambulance medical module providing oxygen, power, and mounting for patient monitoring equipment,” the release also notes. “Merlin believes there is a clear follow-on path to operational scale using a [Beechcraft] King Air variant, which would provide twin-engine redundancy, greater payload capacity, and additional cabin space for multiple litter patients, medical equipment, and an in-flight attendant. The same architecture could also support autonomous logistics and personnel movement across dispersed operating locations.”

As already mentioned, the use case for autonomous CASEVAC capabilities to support U.S. operations in Africa is clear-cut. The scale and scope of AFRICOM operations means that American forces are often dispersed in small groups at far-flung operating locations far from higher-level medical care. Options for getting individuals to a hospital, even after accidents in relatively low-risk areas, can be extremely limited. Medical professionals often talk about the so-called “golden hour,” which refers to the first 60 minutes after a serious injury occurs. The chances of saving that person’s life or otherwise preventing serious permanent damage are highest within that window.

“AFRICOM’s area of responsibility spans vast distances, and security threats can prevent access to nearby medical facilities, often forcing longer and more dangerous patient transport. In these conditions, transporting a wounded noncombatant or service member to medical care is both time-critical and logistically complex,” Merlin says in its release. “Conventional casualty evacuation relies on crewed aircraft, while remotely piloted systems require persistent command-and-control links that may be unavailable in austere or contested environments. The challenge set forth by AFRICOM seeks autonomous solutions that can accelerate access to a higher level of care while reducing the number of personnel exposed to risk.”

This was all rammed home in a very public fashion nearly a decade ago by the infamous ambush of American forces near Tongo Tongo in Niger, in which four U.S. Army soldiers died. The only immediate aerial CASEVAC support available in that instance was provided by contractors operating from the Nigerien capital Niamey more than 100 miles away.

Issues relating to ready access to higher-level medical care, as well as contested logistics chains, together with what is commonly referred to as the ‘‘tyranny of distance,’ are not limited to U.S. operations in Africa. Any high-end fight against China in the Pacific could easily see American forces spread across very broad areas, with established facilities of any kind being few and far between.

Furthermore, the U.S. Marine Corps and the U.S. Air Force, in particular, are envisioning future operations in that region being conducted in a highly distributed manner utilizing austere forward operating locations to create targeting complications for the enemy. The war with Iran has only underscored the kinds of threats and logistics challenges U.S. forces should expect to be faced with in an even larger-scale conflict in the Pacific.

With all this in mind, the U.S. Air Force has already been experimenting with Cessna Grand Caravans with semi-autonomous capabilities as a path to new distributed logistics capabilities, including in the Pacific.

As noted earlier on, Merlin, specifically, has been working for years now to demonstrate new degrees of autonomy in other existing U.S. aircraft. In September, Merlin and Textron (which owns the Cessna brand) also announced a new partnership to develop a cargo-carrying drone derived from the Cessna 408 SkyCourier.

All that being said, the planned AFRICOM autonomous CASEVAC demonstration, and the paltry amount of funding put toward it, highlights how the U.S. military has been lagging behind in this arena.

China, especially, has been surging forward in the development of fully uncrewed logistics aircraft, which could be adapted for aeromedical and other missions in the future. Several Chinese cargo drone designs are flying now, including types that are significantly larger and more capable than a Cessna Grand Caravan. China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be faced with its own logistical and other challenges in any future conflict in the Pacific region.

In recent months, Ukraine has also demonstrated uncrewed CASEVAC capabilities in support of real combat operations using large multi-rotor drones. The U.S. military has explored broadly similar platforms in the past. However, these uncrewed aerial systems are designed for much more localized operations compared to what AFRICOM is now looking to demonstrate in Morocco.

The outcome of the upcoming demonstration of the Merlin Pilot-equipped Cessna Caravan could help spur further interest within the U.S. military in new autonomous aerial CASEVAC and logistics platform. At the same time, it shows U.S. military efforts to pursue these capabilities remain limited despite the clear use cases and already being made by America’s chief global competitor China.

The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.

This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity."

Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry."

evening.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
evening.text:
The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.

This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.

To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.

In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

evening.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
evening.text:
It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.  

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations. 

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage. 

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.  

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035. 

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be. 

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

evening.title: NSG Commandos to Get New Breathable Uniforms After Heatstroke Incident
evening.text:
Intense heat leading to exhaustion has prompted the National Security Guard (NSG) to recommend a new “breathable” uniform for its black cat commandos providing VIP security to some high-risk personalities in the country.
Sources in the security establishment told PTI that the move was prompted by an incident in April when a commando deployed in the close protection security of Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu fainted.
It was almost 44 degrees that day in Vijayawada when the commando wearing a bullet proof jacket over his black overall uniform, a black beret on his head along with small arms holstered around his waist suffered heatstroke and exhaustion, the officials said.
Videos widely circulated of the incident show Naidu speaking to the press when the flanking commando faints and had to be helped by other security personnel to prevent him from falling.
Commanders of the NSG close protection force (CPF) and experts at NSG headquarters viewed the incident seriously and came to a conclusion that the increasing hot weather and rising temperature were taking a physical toll on the VIP security teams of the force.
The black overalls absorb a lot of heat and the commandos have to top it up with an about 6 kg weighing bullet proof vest apart from black sunglasses and communication equipment on their person while on duty, the sources said.
“It has therefore been decided to provide the commandos with better clothing for their uniforms.
“A breathable material named nyco, comprising nylon and cotton, has been recommended for the black uniforms of NSG VIP security commandos,” a source told PTI.
Nycon allows air and moisture vapour to pass through freely keeping the person cool, the sources said.

evening.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
evening.text:
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time.

Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go.

The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal.

Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration.

The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for.

Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places.

That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory.

Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds.

For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit, but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro.

The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal.

Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones.

The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

evening.title: Indian and Pakistani Workers Face Different Defence Project Access in German Defence Companies
evening.text:
A Pakistani professional working for a German company claims to have been excluded from a defence project due to his nationality despite holding permanent residency and the correct visa(s). His story which was posted onto the Reddit r/Pakistan subreddit highlights how security and nationality restrictions are becoming increasingly significant for defence companies looking to increase output and work with multiple countries on military projects.
“I was hired from Pakistan a few years ago and have worked on a couple of different big German companies. But now my employer has won a contract with a new defence project that involves collaboration between the US, Canada and multiple European countries I found out I wouldn’t be able to work on the project.”
As Pakistan was one of the many restricted nationalities (along with Iran, Russia, China, Vietnam) I was unable to work on the project. My Indian colleague was able to sign the NDA and work on the project but I was given no role despite having permanent residency in Germany.
My Indian colleague was given their own room with blackout windows.
Although the name of the German company, defence contractor, project and the exact security restrictions aren’t mentioned. There is no independent evidence that this restriction was put into place by German intelligence. This simply shows that this individual had an issue with being restricted.
The German defence sector has become increasingly targeted by espionage and theft of technology as the country ramps up its military spending and defence manufacturing. In April 2026, Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) warned there is an increase in espionage, sabotage and cyber attacks on defence companies and critical technologies.
This was brought to light again in November after it was reported that Jensen Huang, chief executive at Nvidia, may have been targeted by foreign intelligence. On the 8th November, Nvidia’s board declared an independent investigation into the matter. German intelligence later issued a warning to business executives about using personal connections to target company leaders. Although, Nvidia has stated they have no reason to believe that any company secrets or national security was compromised. The allegations are currently being investigated.
Security clearances in Germany can also play a factor in this situation. The German Security Clearance Act (Sicherheitsüberprüfungsgesetz) allows for individuals to be assessed based on their nationality, former nationalities, time spent living abroad and other personal factors. Extra checks can also be made if the individual is a foreign national. This doesn’t mean that non-Germans cannot obtain a security clearance. However, whilst someone may be legally living and working in Germany they may not be eligible to view certain information.
This can be due to the security restrictions placed on the project. This can cause problems for professionals from Pakistan, as whilst they may have permanent residency they may not be eligible to work on certain sensitive defence projects.Permanent residency allows individuals to live and work in Germany but doesn’t guarantee they will be able to obtain a security clearance from the defence customer, partner government or those originating the classified information.

evening.title: BSF Plans New Drone Simulation and Maintenance Facility in Bengaluru
evening.text:
The Border Security Force (BSF) has issued a tender of ₹49.3 lakh to set up its own drone simulators, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) centre at the BSF’s CEDCO facility in Bengaluru. The procurement, issued by the BSF Signal Training School, comes under the Ministry of Home Affairs, and involves various pieces of equipment including Virtual Reality (VR) Headset, Drone Simulator Software, Radio Controllers, Computer Workstations and Networking Equipment.
The tender was issued on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) on 5 th November 2026. This Tender has the reference number: GEM/2026/B/8199242. The estimated cost of the procurement is ₹49,30,899. Bids must be submitted by 26 th November at 14:00.
This tender will be to ‘To establish drone simulation, maintenance, repair and overhaul, drone lab at CEDCO BSF as turnkey project’. This is part of the BSF’s efforts to develop its drone capabilities. Below are the 9 components to be procured:
The Bill of Quantities (BOQ) details there to be 9 different items within this procurement. In total there will be 45 units to be procured. These are: Computer Workstation, VR Headset , 24 Port Layer 3 Switch , Instructor Podium with Console , 86″ Interactive Flat Panel , 5kva Online UPS with 120 minutes backup , Drone Simulator Software, Radio Controllers, Installation and Commissioning.
This shows there will be a heavy focus on simulating training. With VR Headset, Simulator Software and Radio Controllers to allow trainees to get familiar with operating simulated drones. The Instructor Console and Large Screen will help with teaching within the facilities.
The inclusion of a large UPS and Networking Equipment shows that this will be a complete training environment.
However, looking at the BOQ, despite the MRO title, it looks like there will not be any traditional drone maintenance equipment. There is no mention of any testing or diagnostic equipment, soldering stations, battery testing equipment, motor testing benches, propeller balancing or drone repair. None of these items were mentioned in the 9 components.
Therefore this procurement looks like it will only focus on the simulation and teaching side of the drone facility. Further procurement may be needed to create a full drone maintenance facility.
Restrictions on Bidding
Another interesting point about this tender is the fact it is restricted to Government sellers. This means that private drone manufacturers, MROs and startups will not be able to bid for this project.
There are some concessions given to Micro and Small Enterprises and Startups. These include some concessions on experience and turnover requirements. However, they will still need to be a government seller.
The procurement also requires bidders to have an average annual turnover of ₹24 Lakh and OEM to have a turnover of ₹196 Lakh. There is also a 3 year experience requirement. The winning bidder will also need to provide a performance guarantee of 5% of the contract value for 38 months.

The BSF has also been investing in drone technology through the Police Technology Innovation Centre and Drone Technology Lab located in Tekanpur at the Rustamji Institute of Technology. This facility has been looking at drones which have been recovered and looking at the technology used in drones along India’s borders. This facility could help the BSF with further simulator training for their Drone Warfare capabilities.
Having the capability to train internally will reduce the dependency on outside companies to help with drones, which the BSF are becoming more reliant on for surveillance and border security.
However, based on the equipment listed within this tender it does look like they will only be focussing on the simulators and not a full MRO. The actual maintenance capability would depend on any further equipment and technical staff required.

evening.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
evening.text:
Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch.

Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products. However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error.

Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch.

In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager.

In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully.

However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually.

It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal.

Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services.

The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling, with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update.

At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time.

evening.text:
Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky.

The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set.

"Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18.

For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website.

According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present.

Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured.

NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot."

Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune.

It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
evening.text:
A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data.

Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes.

Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum.

You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated.

YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data.

The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses.

Millions more

HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users.

The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match.

Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB.

NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank, Russia's largest private bank. ®

evening.title: China Takes Notice of India’s Gaganyaan and Space Station Plans
evening.text:
India’s plans to build a space station and put humans into orbit are drawing attention from Chinese commentators and social media users. India often comes up when talking about defence and strategy but interest in India’s space capabilities is rising. As New Delhi move forwards with their Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission and plans for a space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), interest from China is growing.
Social media posts from China have been talking about how India is building their indigenous space station, what timeframe they are looking to launch in and the challenges they face. Some Chinese commentators have said that India are trying to match China’s human spaceflight capabilities but others have questioned if they can actually meet their targets.
There have been videos discussing India’s space station and whether they have the technology, funds and capabilities to achieve this.
While some of these are genuine questions that need to be asked there is lots of interest in India’s space programme. It is becoming clear that India are developing a new capability and this is being talked about. India’s plans are no longer just theoretical. They have had Union Cabinet approval to begin development of the first module (BAS-01) in September 2024.
The Indian Space Research Organisation has confirmed they will have a five module station. The first module will be launched by 2028 and the full Bharatiya Antariksh Station will be fully operational by 2035.
In March 2026 the Department of Space confirmed they were moving forwards with system engineering and sub-system development for BAS-01. The government has also estimated that it will cost ₹1,763 crore to develop and launch the first module.
Before India can have a space station they need to prove they can get humans into orbit and return them safely.
This is where the Gaganyaan programme will come into play. ISRO are preparing multiple unmanned missions to test the launch vehicle, crew module, escape system, life support systems and recovery. China already have a space station (Tiangong), meaning they have lots of experience with humans in orbit, living in space for long periods of time, space walks and resupply.
India are entering a market where China already have a capability but their programme is being built around their launch capabilities, industry and science priorities. This means it isn’t a race to see who can get a space station up first but has its own unique capabilities.
The Chinese interest in India’s plans highlights how India’s space capabilities are being viewed differently. While they have previously been known for being a cheap option for launching satellites and planetary missions they are now working towards independent human spaceflight and a modular research station in orbit.

Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python
evening.text:
"Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work.

Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors.

The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE, short for the XLA Serving Engine.

One-shot inference

XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google.

"LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach, Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday.

At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search.

These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing.

A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory.

No Python here

In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel."

Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here.

XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators.

Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch. Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime, which supports an open graph format with Python bindings.

Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

evening.title: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
evening.text:
UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better.

Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem.

There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd, an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT. Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear.

Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands.

The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery.

Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic."

So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

evening.title: AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM
evening.text:
AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server.

This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter.

AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs.

"Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained.

Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue

Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity."

Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower.

This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window.

So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk.

The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.)

"We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM."

So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext."

To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms.

"The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. So long as the pages are in DRAM before they're needed, the pages don't even need to be in the right order, he added.

Training the models to predict memory access patterns accurately presents its own challenges, which, Smerdon says, makes pre-training the models impractical.

Instead, they take a single Epyc core and train the model "in under one second," he explained. From there, the model is further refined and retrained over time until it is able to predict accurately where the pages need to be and when they need to be there.

All of this training, he emphasizes, takes place on the CPU core — no GPU required, which means essentially any Epyc customer can take advantage of the software platform.

While no GPU may be required, it's worth noting that in virtualized environments, the software requires one core per VM or VPC, so the overhead scales with virtualization. Container runtimes presumably don't suffer from this same limitation. We've reached out to AMD for clarification.

99 percent of the perf, half the DRAM

According to AMD, the technology actually works. Initially, Smerdon says, the company targeted memory-hungry applications like electronic design automation (EDA) and content creation, but later expanded to support latency-sensitive applications like databases and agentic AI pipelines.

"When pages of memory are cold, we can push them off to flash, and there's literally no impact on performance," he said.

Smerdon is overstating things just a little here. Depending on the application and how much memory is offloaded to flash, there is a performance penalty.

According to tests against Synopsys' PrimeTime EDA suite, he claims, half the memory can be offloaded to flash using Mext and the system still achieves 95 percent of the performance of DRAM. With 25 percent DRAM and 75 percent flash, performance fell to 80 percent of the DRAM-only baseline in AMD's tests.

EDA tools are extremely memory-hungry, but the amount of data the cores are working on at any given moment is often measured in megabytes. This is why AMD's Epyc X-chips remain so popular with EDA customers and why Mext targeted it initially.

In other scenarios, like Apache Spark, AMD's Mext team says it is seeing 99 percent of the performance even after replacing half the DRAM in the system with flash.

While implementing the tech may cost some performance, AMD is betting that customers will be willing to make that compromise in exchange for substantial DRAM savings, as memory remains constrained thanks to the AI datacenter buildout.

Right now, AMD is working to integrate Mext into its broader enterprise portfolio. The software, we're told, will be exclusive to AMD hardware and will be offered as a license sold through OEM partners.

Systems running Linux require only a kernel driver to take advantage of the software, while a separate RAM View application is being offered to help enterprises understand which systems and workloads it should be enabled on.

The chip designer says it's currently in the first phase of its Mext rollout, which means working with OEMs like HPE to ensure systems are so-called "Mext ready." In the second phase, the company aims to begin selling licenses for the software and shipping Epyc platforms with RAM View preinstalled.®

evening.title: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home
evening.text:
The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech.

A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered.

A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft.

In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending.

Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers.

And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole.

Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were.

Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships.

One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff, which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available.

That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete.

The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical.

The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip.

Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI.

Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet. The UK should be working with other middle powers, pooling our buying power to shape markets and using shared leverage to secure access to frontier AI."

Darren Jones MP, who wrote the report's foreword, made a similar argument, saying Britain should work with international allies rather than attempting to build everything itself.

"We can change how the state buys technology, back industries where the UK has a genuine opportunity to lead the world, and shape markets – but we can't go it alone. We need to join with natural allies like France, Germany, Japan and Korea and make ourselves indispensable together," he said.

Whitehall might have grand plans for digital sovereignty, but it's going to be a tough sell when so much of its technology comes from across the Atlantic. And with AI already bundled into software contracts worth billions, US tech giants aren't making it easy for the government to shop elsewhere. ®

evening.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
evening.text:
In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior.

“As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post.

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.”

The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster.

“The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises.

A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.”

OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one.

The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development.

“Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.”

OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.”

That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

evening.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime
evening.text:
Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models.

Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks.

Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI.

That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.”

Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”

The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons.

One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things:

  1. Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment

  2. Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models

  3. Allow independent evaluation of their models

  4. Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly

  5. Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency

  6. Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more.

The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism.

Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore.

Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages.

Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment.

Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under.

Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread.

Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years. The organizer was blissfully ignorant of those facilities and eventually said their group is opposed to AI in all forms. ®
